Spring Bean Lifecycle

The Spring Bean Lifecycle is the complete sequence of steps that the Spring IoC container executes from the moment it creates a bean to the moment it destroys it. Understanding this lifecycle lets you hook into exactly the right phase — whether you need to validate configuration after injection, war

Stage-by-Stage Deep Dive
Stage 1 — Instantiation (Constructor)

Spring calls the bean's constructor (or a factory method) to create the object instance. If you have multiple constructors, Spring uses the one annotated with @Autowired , or the single no-arg constructor by default. At this point no dependencies have been injected — the object is just allocated. im
Stage 2 — Populate Properties (Setter / Field Injection)

After construction, Spring resolves all @Autowired fields and setter methods. It also applies values from @Value expressions. This is when the bean's dependency graph is fully satisfied. import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotatio
Stage 3 — BeanNameAware.setBeanName()

If the bean implements BeanNameAware , Spring calls setBeanName(String name) passing the bean's registered name in the container. This is the first of the Aware interface callbacks and fires immediately after property population. import org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanNameAware;
import org.spr
Stage 4 — BeanClassLoaderAware.setBeanClassLoader()

BeanClassLoaderAware gives the bean a reference to the ClassLoader used to load it. This is useful for frameworks that need to dynamically load classes by name using the same classloader as the bean. import org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanClassLoaderAware;
import org.springframework.stereotype
Stage 5 — BeanFactoryAware.setBeanFactory()

BeanFactoryAware injects the owning BeanFactory into the bean. This lets a bean programmatically retrieve other beans from the container — though this is generally an anti-pattern since it couples your code to the Spring API. Prefer constructor injection. import org.springframework.beans.BeansExcept
Stage 6 — EnvironmentAware.setEnvironment()

EnvironmentAware provides the bean with the Environment object, which gives access to property sources, profiles, and system properties. Useful for infrastructure beans that need to read configuration values programmatically. import org.springframework.context.EnvironmentAware;
import org.springfram
Stage 7 — ApplicationContextAware.setApplicationContext()

ApplicationContextAware is the most commonly used Aware interface. It injects the full ApplicationContext , giving access to the entire bean registry, event publishing, message sources, and resource loading. A common pattern is a static holder so non-Spring code can access the context. import org.sp
Stage 8 — BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization()

BeanPostProcessor is a container extension point: implementations are called for every bean in the context, not just beans that implement a specific interface. The postProcessBeforeInitialization hook fires after the Aware callbacks but before the bean's own init methods. You can return the original
Stage 9 — @PostConstruct / InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()

Two hooks fire at this stage in order: the JSR-250 @PostConstruct method first, then InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet() . Both run after all dependencies have been injected. Use them to perform any initialization that requires access to injected dependencies — warming caches, opening connections,
Stage 10 — Custom init-method

A custom init method fires after afterPropertiesSet() . Declare it on a @Bean definition with initMethod , or in XML with init-method . This lets you hook lifecycle behavior into third-party classes you can't annotate. import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.co
Stage 11 — BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization()

The second BeanPostProcessor hook fires after all init callbacks complete. This is when AOP proxies are typically installed — if the bean needs to be wrapped, the proxy replaces the original instance in the container from this point on. The object returned here is what callers will receive when they
Stage 12 — Bean Ready (In Use)

At this point the bean is fully initialized and stored in the container. Calls to applicationContext.getBean() or any injection point will receive this bean (or its proxy). The bean remains in this state until the container begins shutdown. import org.springframework.context.annotation.AnnotationCon
Stage 13 — @PreDestroy / DisposableBean.destroy()

When the container is closed (e.g., context.close() or JVM shutdown hook), Spring calls destroy callbacks in reverse order. The @PreDestroy method fires first, then DisposableBean.destroy() . Use these to release resources: close database connections, flush caches, stop background threads. import ja
Stage 14 — Custom destroy-method

A custom destroy method fires after DisposableBean.destroy() . Declare it on a @Bean with destroyMethod . Spring also has a convention: if a bean has a close() or shutdown() method and no destroyMethod is specified, Spring infers it automatically for @Bean declarations. // Already shown in Stage 10
Scope Comparison: Singleton vs Prototype

Bean scope fundamentally changes how much of the lifecycle the container manages. Singleton beans enjoy full lifecycle management. Prototype beans are handed off to the caller after creation — the container does not track them after that point. Aspect Singleton Prototype Created Once per container N
ApplicationContext vs BeanFactory

ApplicationContext is a superset of BeanFactory . In practice you always use ApplicationContext — the only reason to use BeanFactory directly is in highly resource-constrained environments (e.g., embedded devices) where eager initialization overhead matters. Changing the Default Port

By default Spring Boot listens on port 8080. To change it, add one line to src/main/resources/application.properties : server.port=8081 Then restart the application. Alternatively, pass it on the command line without touching the file: ./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.arguments=--server.port
5. Spring Boot DevTools — Hot Reload

DevTools monitors the JVM classpath for changes and triggers a fast restart — not a full JVM restart. It keeps the JVM alive, swaps only the application's own classes (the app classloader), and restarts the Spring context. This typically takes 1–3 seconds vs 5–20 seconds for a cold start.
Add to pom.xml

<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>
application.properties

# Enable classpath watcher and restart on change
spring.devtools.restart.enabled=true

# Enable LiveReload server (port 35729) — browser extension triggers refresh
spring.devtools.livereload.enabled=true
How It Works

DevTools starts a file watcher on the classpath (your compiled classes). When your IDE saves and compiles a changed class, the watcher detects the update. DevTools discards the application classloader and creates a new one, reloading only your code (third-party library classes are kept). The Spring

7. Actuator Endpoints

Spring Boot Actuator exposes operational information about a running application. By default only /actuator/health is exposed over HTTP. Expose additional endpoints via application.yml : management:
